content: Maternal colonization with Group B Streptococcus (GBS) during pregnancy increases the risk of neonatal infection through vertical transmission from mother to baby. Administering intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis (IAP) during labor has been associated with a reduction in early-onset GBS disease (EOGBSD). However, treating all women who are colonized with GBS during labor exposes a large number of mothers and infants to potential adverse effects without guaranteed benefit. The objective of this review was to evaluate the impact of intrapartum antibiotics for maternal GBS colonization on mortality from any cause, mortality specifically due to GBS infection, and mortality from infections caused by organisms other than GBS. The search for relevant studies was updated on March 11, 2014, using the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register. Randomized controlled trials that assessed the effect of maternal IAP on neonatal GBS infections were included in the analysis. The eligibility and quality of the studies were independently assessed. No new trials were identified in the updated search, so the results remain unchanged. Four trials involving a total of 852 women were included in the review. Three of these trials, which involved 500 women, compared the use of IAP to no treatment. The use of IAP did not significantly reduce the incidence of all-cause mortality, mortality from GBS infection, or mortality from infections caused by bacteria other than GBS. However, IAP was associated with a reduction in the incidence of early-onset GBS infection compared to no treatment. Specifically, the risk ratio (RR) was 0.17 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.04 to 0.74) based on data from three trials involving 488 infants. The risk difference was -0.04 (95% CI -0.07 to -0.01), and the number needed to treat (NNT) to prevent one case of early-onset GBS infection was 25 (95% CI 14 to 100). There was no significant difference in the incidence of late-onset disease (LOD), sepsis caused by organisms other than GBS, or maternal puerperal infection between the groups. One trial involving 352 women compared the use of intrapartum ampicillin versus penicillin. This study found no significant differences in neonatal or maternal outcomes between the two antibiotics. The review identified a high risk of bias in one or more key domains of the study methodology and execution. This raises concerns about the reliability of the findings. The authors concluded that while intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis appeared to reduce the incidence of early-onset GBS disease, this result may be influenced by bias due to methodological limitations in the included studies. There is insufficient evidence from well-designed and rigorously conducted trials to recommend the routine use of IAP to reduce neonatal EOGBSD. Ideally, the effectiveness of IAP in reducing neonatal GBS infections should be evaluated in adequately powered, double-blind, controlled trials. However, the opportunity to conduct such trials may have been lost, as many jurisdictions have already implemented practice guidelines recommending IAP, despite the lack of robust evidence.
